gap: No result ChatGPT got that I could open states how many watt-hours these 2 kWh units deliver in named tests: FOSSiBOT F2400 1,512 Wh (Techtest, 100 W AC) and 1,659 Wh (nextpit), against about 1,800 Wh (Notebookcheck, 250 W AC) and 1,870 Wh (StorageReview) for the Anker SOLIX F2000 and 1,710-1,740 Wh (OutdoorGearLab) for the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2.
standout_why: I compared against cheapestwh.com (cited, opened 2026-11-11). It ranks only by rated capacity and says "we do not test units ourselves"; it has no measured Wh, efficiency, noise or charge time for any unit. The three cited outletpicks.com URLs, powerstationgearlab.com and our own dealectric.com page could not be opened (WebFetch certificate error, shell denied), so I could not check them. That is why this is 2 and not 3. ChatGPT's own answer compares only rated Wh and rated $/Wh.
decides: It weakens ChatGPT's 'best overall value' call for the FOSSiBOT F2400. At the $599 ChatGPT showed for both, the Anker F2000 delivered about 140-210 Wh more in named tests (1,800-1,870 Wh against 1,659 Wh) and charged in under 1.5 h against 2.5-2.75 h. Using ChatGPT's prices, cost per delivered Wh is about $0.32-0.33 for the Anker, $0.34 for the Jackery and $0.36-0.40 for the FOSSiBOT, so the tie on rated $/Wh disappears. The F2400 stays the pick only if the Anker and Jackery third-party deals cannot be verified; cheapestwh lists the Jackery at $999 on Amazon today and does not list the F2000. The cheapest card, DYNESS, has no named measurement at all. The tests used different loads and labs, so the gap is indicative rather than exact.

findings.label: Usable energy via AC outlet at 100 W load (Techtest.org, Michael Barton)
findings.source_title: FOSSiBOT F2400 Powerstation Test: Leistung, Kapazität und Effizienz im Überblick
findings.note: Published 2024-07-03. This is the low end of the article's 1,512-1,807 Wh range. A 100 W load is a worst case because inverter overhead is a large share of it. 1,512/2,048 = 73.8%.

findings.label: Usable energy via USB-C at 100 W (Techtest.org, Michael Barton)
findings.source_title: FOSSiBOT F2400 Powerstation Test: Leistung, Kapazität und Effizienz im Überblick
findings.note: Published 2024-07-03. DC discharge bypasses the inverter. 1,807/2,048 = 88.2%.

findings.label: Measured AC charge time (Techtest.org, Michael Barton)
findings.value: about 2 h 45 min at the 1,100 W setting; 3 h 45 min at 700 W
findings.source_title: FOSSiBOT F2400 Powerstation Test: Leistung, Kapazität und Effizienz im Überblick
findings.note: Published 2024-07-03. The author saw brief charging dropouts after about 30 minutes at 1,100 W and suspects thermal throttling. From a 12-13 V car source the unit drew about 100 W at most.

findings.label: Energy in and out over a full cycle (nextpit, Thomas Kern)
findings.value: 2,127 Wh from the wall to charge; 1,659 Wh delivered; 78% round trip
findings.note: Published 2023-12-19. Discharge load not stated in the article. 1,659/2,127 = 78.0%; 1,659/2,048 = 81.0% of rated. The same article quotes 85% for the Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus.

findings.label: Charge time and fan noise (nextpit, Thomas Kern)
findings.value: 2.5 h full charge (maker claims 2 h); 55 dB
findings.note: Published 2023-12-19. Measuring distance for the 55 dB figure is not given.

findings.label: Runtime with a 290 W gaming laptop (Notebookcheck, Christian Hintze)
findings.value: about 6 hours at 290 W average draw
findings.source_title: Leistungsstarke 2.400-W-Powerstation mit unterbrechungsfreier Stromversorgung: FossiBot F2400 im Test
findings.note: Published 2025-05-27, page updated 2026-10-05. 290 W × 6 h ≈ 1,740 Wh is my arithmetic, not a Notebookcheck figure. The article gives no usable-capacity, noise or idle measurement.

findings.label: Usable energy via AC at about 250 W continuous (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten)
findings.value: around 1,800 Wh over a good 7 hours (about 88% of rated 2,048 Wh)
findings.source_title: Anker PowerHouse 767 in practice test: Powerstation flagship is still a mobile powerhouse
findings.note: Published 2023-01-14. Tested on the 230 V EU unit. 1,800/2,048 = 87.9%.

findings.label: Charge energy, charge efficiency, charge time and noise (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten)
findings.value: 2,309 Wh to charge; just under 89% charging efficiency; 80% in about 1 h, full in just under 1.5 h; up to 55 dB while charging at about 2,000 W
findings.source_title: Anker PowerHouse 767 in practice test: Powerstation flagship is still a mobile powerhouse
findings.note: Published 2023-01-14. Round trip by my arithmetic: 1,800/2,309 = 78.0%, the same as nextpit's figure for the F2400, so the Anker's edge is in delivered Wh and charge speed, not round-trip efficiency. The EU unit charges at up to 2,200 W; the US 120 V unit's input differs.

findings.label: Charge and discharge energy (StorageReview, Jordan Ranous)
findings.value: 2,300 Wh to charge 0-100%; 1,870 Wh discharged before inverter cutoff
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F2000 Portable Power Station Review
findings.note: Published 2023-12-14. Discharge load not stated. 1,870/2,048 = 91.3% of rated; 1,870/2,300 = 81.3% round trip (my arithmetic).

findings.label: Measured AC energy output (OutdoorGearLab, Chris McNamara and Kenji Mowrey)
findings.value: 1,710 Wh in the spec table, 1,740 Wh in the text; 84% of advertised 2,042 Wh
findings.note: Published 2025-11-03. The page's two figures conflict: 1,710/2,042 = 83.7%, 1,740/2,042 = 85.2%. Tested via AC outlets; the review calls 84% about average for its test group.

findings.label: Measured charge time, charge rate and weight (OutdoorGearLab)
findings.note: Published 2025-11-03. No decibel figure. The spec table lists a 2-year warranty.

findings.label: Inverter efficiency, standby draw and surge (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 90% efficiency; about 17 W with the inverter on and no load (roughly 5 days to empty); surge about 3,100 W; AC input about 1,300 W outside Emergency Charging Mode
findings.source_title: Jackery Explorer 2000 V2 Review: Should You Buy It or the 2000 Plus?
findings.note: Page shows no publication date or author name. Load for the 90% figure is not stated. It sits above OutdoorGearLab's 84%, so the two are not directly comparable.
